title: Earth’s CO2 rises and falls every year because most of its plants are in the north
body: Measured on Mauna Loa in Hawaiʻi, carbon dioxide swings up and down by **about 6 ppm** every year on top of its long climb. It peaks in May, falls through the northern spring and summer as plants grow and take up CO2, bottoms out in September, and rises again through autumn and winter. The north sets the rhythm because that is where most of the land, and so most of the vegetation, is.

slides.question: In which month does carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa usually reach its yearly high?
slides.explanation: It peaks in May, then falls through the northern spring and summer to a low in September, and rises again in autumn and winter.

slides.prompt: Who began taking regular CO2 measurements on Mauna Loa, and when?
slides.detail: He was the first to make frequent, regular measurements there, and the record he started is called the Keeling Curve.
